Hi Alex — great to hear the call was useful. Quick recap and next steps below, plus a short checklist attached.

Recap (Private VPC path):
- Redwood Private supports both AWS PrivateLink and VPC peering for our managed control plane connectivity; for on-prem we offer an IP allowlist + mutual TLS option.
- Inference traffic runs over a customer-dedicated endpoint in your VPC (either via Privatelink ENI or peering + NAT depending on your topology). Telemetry (metrics/traces) can be routed to your metrics endpoint or forwarded to our control plane over the PrivateLink connection. We can isolate telemetry on a separate subdomain if required.

Immediate asks for your ops team (what we need to start a technical qualification):
1) Preferred connectivity option: PrivateLink or VPC Peering? Indicate reasons (security/regulatory or networking constraints).
2) CIDR(s) for your VPC where the ENI will be created (or the subnet pool for peering).
3) Any restrictive egress/NAT rules that could block outbound TLS on standard ports (443).
4) Point of contact in your cloud team + scheduling 30–45m troubleshooting window during initial provisioning.

I've attached a short "Redwood Private — networking checklist" that includes egress IPs and a sample allowlist we commonly use. See attached: redwood-networking-checklist.pdf.

Next steps: if you confirm Preferred option + CIDRs, I will loop our connectivity engineer (Karthik) and have him provide an exact list of IPs and the per-region ENI ranges.

Best regards,
Mina Haddad

Hi Mina / Alex — thanks for the context. Below are the concrete answers and a short acceptance checklist you can hand to cloud ops.

1) PrivateLink vs VPC peering — short guidance:
- Recommend PrivateLink when the customer requires minimal routing complexity and wants to avoid cross-account route table changes; it provides ENI-based private connectivity and better isolation for control-plane calls. Good for SOC2 requirements because traffic traverses AWS network without exposing public IPs.
- Recommend VPC peering when you need lower latency and want direct VPC-to-VPC routing; peering can be simpler if both accounts are managed by the same org and you accept route-table updates. Not suitable if you need central egress allowlisting without NAT.

2) Egress IPs / Allowlist specifics (per-region):
- For us-east-1 (example): 34.200.12.45, 34.200.12.46, 34.200.12.47
- For us-west-2 (example): 52.23.88.101, 52.23.88.102
- NOTE: these are allocated ENI addresses we bind during provisioning; we will provide the final exact list once you confirm region(s) and model corridor (sequence length/throughput impacts pool sizing).

3) Telemetry separation:
- Telemetry can be routed via the same PrivateLink connection but on a separate DNS subdomain (metrics.redwood.private). If QuantEdge prefers to ingest metrics on-prem or to a private Prometheus endpoint, we can forward via a customer-managed metrics relay inside your VPC — this avoids sending telemetry to our control plane.

4) Acceptance checklist (short):
- Control plane connectivity validated via PrivateLink ENI to specified subnets (confirmation of ENI creation).
- Security team has confirmed allowlist entries for the provided egress IPs.
- TLS egress (443) allowed from Redwood ENIs to your metrics endpoint if you want telemetry forwarded.
- Capacity test: run a 10-minute synthetic inference workload (we'll coordinate) and validate latency and token throughput targets.
- Audit logs: ensure that retention policy for request logs meets your retention window; we can ship logs to your S3 bucket if required.

Next steps: Alex — if you confirm (a) preferred connectivity option (PrivateLink preferred for SOC2), (b) target region(s) and the subnet/CIDR for ENI placement, we will send a final egress IP list and propose two slots next week for the provisioning call (30–45m).

Happy to jump on a call to walk the ops team through the checklist.

—Karthik
Connectivity Engineer, Redwood Inference
